title: Market Pulse (Open Access)
body_html:
This post reflects my current views on the market, sectors, and internal breadth/momentum. Expect candid, data-driven analysis, peppered with personal insights drawn from years of trading experience. I aim to provide value in every edition, helping you to see the market through a clearer, more informed lens.

What You Can Expect

  • In-Depth Market Analysis: A thorough examination of market trends, key indices, and pivotal turning points.

  • Sector Spotlights: A closer look at the hottest (and not-so-hot) sectors, highlighting opportunities and risks.

  • Breadth and Momentum Insights: Understanding the underlying strength of the market through breadth indicators and momentum metrics.

Exclusive Features

  • Interactive Spreadsheet: Alongside each post, I’ll be linking a detailed spreadsheet that tracks the breadth and momentum metrics. This will allow you to follow along with the data and see the trends I’m analyzing in real-time.

  • Quick Video Commentary: To complement the metrics, I’ll also be posting a quick video commentary on most days. This will provide a more dynamic overview of the market, offering you additional context and clarity.

Market Metrics

Overall: Negative

The market has shifted from being indecisive to making a clear choice—but for now, that choice is to the downside. After some back-and-forth movement, all four major indices have dipped below their 20-day moving averages, a level that often indicates who’s holding the advantage. In this case, sellers have gained some control, and the market is experiencing a bit more pressure.

This shift includes individual sectors as well. Even the last few sectors that had been holding up have now joined in the broader pullback, suggesting that this is a more widespread, market-wide adjustment rather than isolated to certain areas.

Internals have also turned more cautious. Breadth has expanded negative, with more stocks declining than advancing, and momentum is expanding downward, confirming the current trend. This alignment of breadth and momentum strengthens the negative weight of evidence.

In summary, while the market has turned downward for now, this isn’t necessarily a “doomsday” scenario. It’s a time to adopt a more cautious approach and continue to prioritize managing risk. Such pullbacks are common and can often help to set up better opportunities when the market stabilizes. When that happens, we don’t need to guess. We just need to wait.

Plan of Action

1. Limit Exposure and Focus on Capital Preservation

  • Hold back on new positions: Given the negative trends across all indices and internals, avoid taking on aggressive positions. The focus should be on capital preservation rather than increasing exposure in a weak environment.

  • Reduce risk on existing positions: Consider trimming or cutting back on any open positions that show weakness or lack follow-through. Focus on maintaining core positions only in stocks that are still holding key levels or showing relative strength.

2. Monitor Key Market Indicators for Signs of Stabilization

  • Track NHs/NLs and momentum: Keep a close watch on new highs vs. new lows and momentum indicators to monitor for any signs of improvement in market internals. For now, a continued negative breadth and momentum trend suggests limited opportunities, but signs of stabilization may indicate when to cautiously re-enter.

  • Look for sector rotation: Even in a weak market, certain sectors may start to show relative strength. Pay attention to any emerging sectors that could provide selective opportunities if the market shows signs of recovery.

3. Stay Defensive and Ready to React

  • Tighten stops on early positions: If testing “feelers” with small positions, keep stops tight and be prepared to exit if they fail to show strong follow-through. Flexibility is essential to managing risk if the market weakness persists.

  • Maintain a high cash position: Staying largely in cash is a defensive stance that provides flexibility to re-enter selectively when conditions improve. This approach minimizes risk while keeping you ready to act when the market becomes more favorable.

4. Focus on Small Position Sizes (If you trade at all)

  • Start small and scale slowly: For any new trades, limit position sizes significantly. If these setups start to show strength, consider scaling gradually but only after confirming clear signs of stability or upward movement.

  • Diversify and avoid concentration risk: Limit exposure in any single trade, focusing on a diversified approach to manage downside risk. Only add to positions that show sustained strength in the face of the overall negative market trend.

5. Reevaluate Regularly and Adjust Accordingly

  • Assess market conditions daily: Given the negative trends, it’s essential to regularly reevaluate the environment and adjust your plan as needed. If the market shows continued weakness, be prepared to remain defensive until conditions indicate a potential turn.

  • Watch for constructive signals before increasing exposure: Only increase exposure if breadth, momentum, and sector trends begin to improve. Clear signs of market stabilization or upward momentum will signal when it may be safer to cautiously re-enter with selective trades.
